newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya unveils drawn-out constitution reform plans.
newsitem.headline: Kenya unveils drawn-out constitution reform plans.

text.p: Kenya's attorney-general unveiled plans on Monday to review the constitution but the protracted timetable fell far short of opposition demands.
Amos Wako published a draft bill to create a commission to review the constitution and said it had up to three years to report to President Daniel arap Moi.

An opposition-backed alliance grouping religious leaders and civic society wants sweeping constitutional reforms within two years to curb presidential powers and create a level political playing field.
The opposition wants other legal reforms and repeal of laws it deems repressive before presidential and general elections due this year. Moi has not yet set the election date.

"This is too long, too long," said Peter Anyang' Nyong'o, a member of parliament for the opposition FORD-Kenya party and a member of the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC) pushing for reforms.
"The commission could do its work in a year. A lot of work has already been done. The government is time-wasting," he told Reuters.
Most foreign diplomats in Nairobi say Moi is favourite to win the elections because the opposition is divided and the rules of the electoral game are heavily tilted in his favour.
Now aged 73 and in power since 1978, Moi will enter his last five-year term if he wins, under the current constitution.
At least nine people were killed on July 7 during a day of clashes between riot police and pro-reform demonstrators in the worst violent political unrest in the country for seven years.
The NCEC has called for a national strike next Friday.
Moi met religious leaders on Monday to discuss changes to Kenya's constitution and the maintenance of peace and security, the official Presidential Press Service said.

Wako's draft bill said: "The commission shall complete its work and submit its report to the president within 24 months from the date of appointment of the commissioners or within such further period not exceeding 12 months after the end of the 24 months from the date of appointment."
The period covering the appointment of the commissioners, a national debate and the approval of reforms by parliament could last at least three-and-a-half years, Wako's draft bill indicated.
It gave at least six months for the commission's report to move from the presidency to parliament.
The president attempted last month to pull the reform rug from under the feet of the opposition by promising some concessions.

On Saturday, Kenya's opposition said it was deeply suspicious of another draft law providing for political reforms as well as anti-corruption measures. The opposition held that the law, published on Friday, did not go far enough on reform.
Wako proposed on Friday amending various laws ranging from banking to public security and repeal of the Vagrancy Act under which police can detain anyone on suspicion of being a vagabond.
Wako on Monday said he wanted the constitutional review commission established under an act of parliament before the elections and it would seek views across the country.
